value.overview: The Black-crowned Antpitta (Pittasoma michleri) is a secretive, ground-dwelling forest bird of Central America and northwestern Colombia. It belongs to the gnateater family, Conopophagidae, rather than the true antpittas. Usually encountered alone or in pairs, it moves quietly through dense understory and leaf litter, where its rounded body, short tail, and richly patterned underparts help it blend into shadowy forest. Its distinctive calls are often easier to detect than the bird itself.
value.classification: The Black-crowned Antpitta is a passerine in the family Conopophagidae and genus Pittasoma. It is one of two recognized species in this genus.
value.identification: This medium-sized bird is about 18–19 cm long. Adults have a dark blackish crown, brown to chestnut sides of the head, olive-brown upperparts, and a chestnut-brown tail and wings. The throat is dark, while the whitish to buff underparts are strongly marked with black, giving the breast and belly a scaled or barred appearance. The bird has a stout bill, longish legs, and a compact, rounded profile. It is more often heard or glimpsed briefly than seen in the open.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from eastern Costa Rica through Panama to northwestern Colombia. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly on the Caribbean slope, especially in humid foothill forests, generally from roughly 300 to 1,000 meters elevation. It favors mature evergreen or wet foothill forest with dense understory, tangled vegetation, and deep leaf litter. It forages close to the ground and may use forest edges or lightly disturbed habitat where dense cover remains, but it is strongly associated with humid forest conditions.
value.migrationStatus: The Black-crowned Antpitta is considered a resident species. In Costa Rica, individuals are present year-round on the Caribbean slope; no regular long-distance migration is recognized.
value.breeding: Reliable, detailed information on the breeding biology of the Black-crowned Antpitta is limited. The species is believed to breed within humid forest across its range. Like other small forest birds that forage near the ground, it likely places its nest in dense vegetation close to the forest floor, but nest structure, clutch size, incubation, and parental care are not sufficiently documented here to describe confidently.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of forest-floor invertebrates, including insects, spiders, scorpions, and other arthropods. It may also take small vertebrates such as frogs and small lizards. The bird searches through leaf litter and low vegetation, using short hops and pauses to locate prey. Its heavy bill and terrestrial habits are well suited to probing, picking, and seizing prey in damp, shaded understory.
value.behavior: The Black-crowned Antpitta is shy, quiet, and highly skulking. It usually stays on or near the ground, moving through dense cover rather than crossing open areas. It often forages alone or in pairs and may remain motionless when approached, making it difficult to observe. Vocalizations can provide the first indication of its presence. The species is most likely to be encountered in undisturbed or well-developed humid forest understory with abundant leaf litter.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well documented. The species is locally uncommon and depends on humid forest, but it is not currently considered globally threatened.
